Introduction - May 2010 











##### **Introduction** 

The dramatic swings noted for all base metal prices during the different acts of what began as a Greek and evolved into a wider Eurozone sovereign debt crisis illustrate the importance the investment component of these markets continues to hold.  Investors in recent weeks have been ‘spooked’ by the possibility that the problems Greece has been facing may spread to other countries.  The violent events that took place during the general strike in Greece further added to concerns that au

sterity measures required to bring public finances around Europe under control may prove impossible to implement. As a result, liquidations were seen across all risky and pro-cyclical assets, that resulted in a collapse across asset classes, with the exception of the US dollar as well as gold (and to some extent other precious metals), which benefited from the ‘flight to quality’ that emerged. The recent announcement of a €720 billion European financial stabilisation mechanism early this week gave markets some respite and fuelled a strong recovery in the euro, equity as well as base metal prices. This proved short-lived, as soon after the initial excitement waned, corrections across the board followed. ###### **Underlying demand growth still remains positive, for** ###### **the time being** While recognising that base metal prices have been dragged down by the sovereign debt crisis, it should be noted that the bulk of the economic data relating to the base metals sector remains broadly supportive. This is particularly the case for data relating to China - industrial production, fixed asset investment, steel production and vehicle production all point on-going strong base metal demand growth within the country. Elsewhere, continued improvements in mature economies and lack of any significant re-stocking to-date in these markets suggest that consumption growth acceleration may emerge in the not too distant future. ###### **~~Base Metals & Other Commodity Prices~~** 250

At the same time, we continue to see considerable downside risks to this broadly positive Base Case scenario. Starting with Europe, although the support mechanism announced recently may provide some protection against potential escalation of debt woes for the other European countries that suffer from problematic finances, the fact remains that in order to reduce deficits countries will have to implement austerity measures. Elsewhere, although the European crisis has diverted attention from it, the United States fiscal imbalances are also a concern. Finally, the possibility that Chinese growth will be hampered by a potential tightening of monetary policy, to avert the economy from overheating, in our view remains real, particularly looking into early 2011. All the above could adversely affect base metal price both directly, through their impact on consumption, and indirectly, as they would likely culminate in liquidations and corrections that would affect all pro-cyclical asset classes. ###### **Latest trends in the steel market send positive signals for base metals** As we have discussed on a number of occasions in our previous research, we view trends in global steel production as a reasonable proxy for the

underlying demand conditions for the base metals sector – this obviously reflects the fact that the steel industry is a significant consumer of base metals and perhaps, more importantly, it shares many of the same end use markets. The latest data from the World Steel Association (WSA) estimates global steel production in March at 92.144 million tonnes, which was 30.6% up on the corresponding month of 2009. Importantly, the strong growth was not just a function of China, where output was up by 24.5% in the first three months at 158 million tonnes. The WSA data also points to strong growth in the EU-27 countries (+37%), Japan (+50.7%) and the United States (+61.5%). ###### **~~Base Metals Prices in Major Currencies~~** 250

In early May, as the Greek sovereign debt crisis intensified, prices fell below $7,000/tonne and are currently trading in the upper $6,000s._** - **_The rate at which LME inventories fell slowed in April and by end-month stocks stood at just under 497,000 tonnes, more than 15,000 tonnes down from end-March._** - **_Imports into China rose above 300,000 tonnes in March for the first time since June last year, in the aftermath of local prices spending the two preceding months at a premium over London._** - **_Early estimates by the WBMS as well as anecdotal information all confirm that mature economies consumption

growth remains modest. Elsewhere, Chinese demand continues to boom._** - **_Under our Base Case, as these issues are overcome, investors focus on the metal’s medium to longer-term fundamentals and fuel a price recovery._** - **_Lacklustre immediate fundamentals expected to continue over the next six months. Independent - Informed - International **C1** Copper - May 2010 ###### **Market Background** The second quarter of the year started on a positive note, as prices extended the gains made in late March, breaking through the $8,000/tonne mark on a few occasions during CESCO week in early April. Strong resistance at that level soon saw prices consolidate to the upper $7,000s, and it was not until late in the month that prices fell below $7,500/ tonne. More recently, a hike in risk aversion related to the outcome of the Greek sovereign debt crisis and the impact this has had on the euro saw prices collapse to an intra-day low of l

ess than $6,700/tonne on 5th May, before a recovery to current levels of a little over $7,100/tonne. The price volatility seen over the last few weeks continues to confirm GFMS’ view that investor activity remains the main driver of copper price movements. Equally supportive of our view was the high correlation noted between copper and most other base metals prices over the period, which exceeded 0.80 for aluminium, lead and zinc and stood at 0.70 and 0.56 against nickel and tin respectively. The rate of the decline in LME inventories slowed in April compared to March, confirming our understanding that any improvements in demand conditions to-date are modest. By end-month stocks had fallen by 15,475 tonnes from their end-March levels, compared to a 38,800 tonne decline during that month. ###### **Sovereign debt crisis behind copper price movements** As discussed in the introduction, developments relating to the Greek sovereign debt crisis have played a key role in base metal price fluctuations recently and copper has been no exception. The main concern continues to be the possibility of contagion, which could see a number of European economies suffer a considerable slow-down, which would hurt an already fragile recovery of copper consumption in these markets. This, in addition to the general “flight to quality” that has seen investors exit a range of pro-cyclical assets and move into cash, has put pressure of copper prices. ###### **~~Copper Premiums Jan 05 - Present~~** 250

###### **Acceleration of demand growth yet to begin** We continue to see little evidence of an acceleration of copper demand growth. Our contact with numerous market participants during CESCO week confirmed that mature economies’ demand growth, although in positive territory, continues to be slow. China, in contrast, is reported to continue to boom, perhaps somewhat surprisingly considering the remarkable increase its consumption experienced last year. Although we acknowledge it is arguably somewhat outdated, only covering January and February figures, and subject to future revisions, the latest WBMS data by and large confirms the uninspiring rate of recovery in ‘western’ copper consumption. Starting with Europe, despite an extremely low base last year, demand over the two months in question only increased by 5.8% according to the WBMS. Looking at the figures in more detail, we believe they likely understate the true level of consumption early this year and expect upward revisions to take place. For instance, German consumption was reported down at the margin. This contradicts our information which suggests growth, albeit modest, has occurred. It is worth noting here that our view of European copper consumption is also in line with recent comm

ents by Aurubis’ CEO, suggesting Europe’s largest producer has experienced a rise in demand for all major types of copper products in the first quarter. Noteworthy increases among the European WBMS numbers were the 37% rise in Russian demand to around 112,000 tonnes, the 46% gain in Polish consumption to nearly 60,000 tonnes and the 39% increase of Swedish offtake. An even bleaker picture is, surprisingly, painted for North American consumption, with the figures for the United States actually suggesting a 7% decline took place during January and February. GFMS are convinced this was not the case and although we expect US consumption to prove historically low in the first quarter, given the exceptionally low base last year we envisage year-on-year growth in the low double digits. ###### **~~Chinese Copper Imports~~** 400

**C2** Independent - Informed - International Copper - May 2010 Moving to China, as we have access to more recent data on the country from Antaike as well as other sources, we estimate first quarter apparent consumption in the country rose by more than a third to 1.8 million tonnes. Compared to the final quarter of last year, the figure was up by a far more modest 5%. The figures compare to semis fabrication growth of 23% year-on-year and a quarter-on-quarter drop of 17%, according to Antaike. As such, it is likely that some unreported stockpiling of metal may have occurred over the period, something which, as we discuss later in this section, would not seem surprising given the local price premium over the LME price during January and February. Nevertheless, it is worth noting that we would expect any additions to unreported stocks over the first quarter to have been limited and certainly far lower than those recorded during parts of last year. ###### **Shangai-London arbitrage boosts March imports** In March, imports of refined metal into China jumped above 300,000 tonnes for the first time since June last year. This was likely the result of the local price premium over London that was in place during much of the preceding two months. Overall, net imports over the first quarter stood at just over 748,000 tonnes, virtually unchanged from last year and up by 32% quarter-on-quarter. Given the experience of last year, we would not be surprised if arbitrage-trading over the period resulted in some off-exchange stock build up, particularly as this fits in well with the above-mentioned difference between apparent consumption and semis production. ###### **Customs regulations changes may shed light on scrap imports** As we discuss in detail in our recently released inaugural _Copper Survey_ , GFMS believe that official statistics for Chinese imports of copper scrap are hard to interpret and not comparable with trade flow statis

tics elsewhere. As such, GFMS tend to look at derived import figures, i.e. partner-country export data. The problems by and large relate to a different and apparently inconsistent over time definition of what comprises copper scrap, be that officially or as a result of unofficial activity. In the latest Antaike report, it was reported that the Chinese customs released a notice suggesting a stricter implementation of classifications and import practices relating to solid wastes. The new regime is set to be implemented starting 1st June and may result in a more transparent view of the local scrap market. At the time of writing, only a very limited amount of data on derived imports of scrap into China during the first quarter was available and this pointed to a noteworthy increase year-on-year. Official reports showed a little less than 1 million tonnes of gross imports during the three-month period, marking a 34% year-on-year increase. Looking at the relevant unit-values and comparing them to the average quarterly copper price suggests that the rise in the coppercontained in the material is likely to have been stronger. ###### **Production continues to grow** Against the backdrop of uninspiring recovery in many key market’s consumption, the latest developments on the production front confirm ongoing growth in output. Starting with China, first quarter refined copper output in the country was up by 16% year-on-year. The increase was fuelled by a 32% rise in local mine production, a 21% lift in imports of concentrates and the likely rise in scrap imports discussed above. In Chile, the world’s largest copper mining country, in late April the country’s National Statistics Institute announced mine production in March was up 5% year-on-year, at just over 451,000 tonnes. This brought first quarter production to 1.269 million tonnes, marking a 2.1% year-on-year increase. Ongoing growth was also seen in Africa, where the WBMS estimates mine production was up by more than 19% during January and February combined, to 208,000 tonnes. The LME Stocks vs Spot Price

of writing the immediate fundamentals of the copper market continue to be uninspiring. Our estimates for the first quarter see a market in surplus, although at 29,000 tonnes its magnitude is far more limited than during last year. Moreover, in our view oversupply is set to remain in place during the next six months and in fact increase, as production continues to ramp up against only modest improvements in consumption. The much discussed tightness in the copper market is only expected to emerge in the final quarter of the year, under our **Base Case Scenario** , as acceleration in mature economies’ demand growth finally sees global consumption catching up and exceeding (albeit only modestly so) refined production. ###### **~~Copper Price & Forecast Trading Range~~** 10000

Despite the above, our projections for copper prices remain by and large benign for the red metal. GFMS continue to see investor activity being the principal driver of copper price fluctuations over the rest of the year. In the very near-term, ongoing turmoil in the sovereign debt arena will likely keep prices under pressure, but as the quarter progresses and “the dust settles”, we envisage a return to the upper-$7,000s, with a breach of the $8,000/tonne mark possible, as investors once again shift their focus to copper’s fundamental outlook. Such a backdrop is likely to continue through to the end of the third quarter, with corrections which will see prices move comfortably below $7,000/tonne expected to be followed by strong buying on dips. Stronger buying is expected to emerge towards the end of the year, as the market begins tightening. As such, we forecast prices to average $7,950/tonne during the final quarter and that by its end levels comfortably above $8,000/tonne will have been achieved on a sustainable basis. The obvious trigger for our bearish **Scenario C** at the moment is the potential for the sovereign debt crisis to spread rapidly to other European nations which are suffering from problematic government finances, the obvious ones being Spain, Portugal and Ireland, as well as the United Kingdom. Coupled with China tightening monetary policy to prevent the country from overheating, such developments could have a major impact on consumption projections. In the medium-term, noteworthy disinvestment as a result of this could see a correction to the low $5,000s. Although from that point we would expect prices to trend upwards, given the lacklustre nature of the recovery in consumption we would forecast under this scenario, gains would likely be limited. Under a more bullish **Scenario B** , the current crisis is swiftly overcome and global markets re-enter their path to recovery. As a result, nickel prices escalated to $27,325/tonne in late April representing a gain of over 40% when comparing to the start of the year. This was also the first time the spot price rose over $27,000/tonne in almost two years. Nevertheless, a comparison with the other LME base metal prices shows that nickel’s rise was somewhat inflated. This is why since the recent peak there has been a correction in prices. Economic problems surrounding Greece and other European countries coupled with a strengthening US dollar have seen investors pull out from the base metals complex, which has added to the downward momentum. Ad

ditionally, the re-emergence of Chinese nickel pig iron production has also taken a toll on prices. At present, the spot price is trading at around $22,800/tonne on May 12th, slightly above the recent low of $21,670/tonne. Meanwhile LME inventories have continued the downward trend that was in place at the time of our last report. They have fallen by over 21,000 tonnes to around 144,000 tonnes since peaking to an all-time high in early February, but they remain high when comparing to even a year ago, for example. Nevertheless, we believe stocks will continue to fall as demand from the stainless producers looks set to remain firm.. ###### **“Western World” continues to climb out of the recession** A number of countries affected severely by the downturn have seen their stainless steel markets pick up since the start of the year. In our last Base Metals One Year Forecast, we highlighted that the recovery in Europe came in faster than expected. Indeed, this trend has continued since then, but more importantly, alongside Europe, the United States has also seen a considerable improvement. In terms of end-use demand in Europe, automotive sector related buying has picked up vastly, with the white goods sector also showing continued improvement, as are stainless intensive applications like sinks and catering. However, commercial building remains subdued. This is not surprising as the housing sector was the most affected by the economic downturn. Acerinox has recently reported its stainless production figures for the first quarter. The Spanish producer produced 535,500 tonnes in this period, up by almost 60% year-onyear. Nearly 44% of sales were in the United States and 42% in Europe, while 9% in Asia. The company is hoping to deliver second quarter results close to pre-crisis levels and is set to maintain production at near 100% capacity at all its plants until July. In the United States, demand for flat products has picked up considerably. In terms of company specific, AK Steel recently reported that total shipments in the first quarter totalled 1.39 million short tons and is expecting shipments to come in 5% higher than this level in the second quarter. ###### **Chinese stainless steel production remains upbeat** While the “Western World” continues to climb out of recession, China also continues to expand. According to the latest data by the General Administration of Custom, imports of stainless flats 600mm or wider grew by 83% year-on-year over the first three months of the year to 205,211 tonnes, while imports of less than 600mm wide increased, although a lot less, by 16% year-on-year to 36,118 tonnes. **N2** Independent - Informed - International Nickel & Cobalt - May 2010 ###### **Global nickel consumption responds to higher stainless steel output** According to the latest data from the World Bureau of Metal Statistics (WBMS), global nickel demand increased by 13.3% over the first two months of the year. However, a monthon-month examination shows that global consumption in February, although up on January, remained down on December, and even November. Nevertheless, every region with the exception of the Americas noted positive growth. Surprisingly, the region was let down by negative growth in the United States. This is certainly at odds with US physical premiums, which have been on an upward trend since the start of the year. More importantly, the WBMS’ estimate does not reflect the fact that stainless steel production in the country has been increasing. By comparison, European demand was, as expected, up year-on-year over January-February. The region registered growth of 19.4%, with the bulk of the Sweden, Finland and Italy being the main drivers behind this growth. Reflecting the improvement, European physical premiums have been increasing since the start of the year. The 4x4 cathode premium is currently in a range of $400-500/tonne up 64% year-to-date. ###### **Japan drives Asian consumption higher** Asian consumption increased by 17.4% year-on-year to 114,100 tonnes. The main driver behind this growth was Japan, which saw its consumption for nickel grow by 66% year-on-year. This comes following a decline of over 20% last year. ###### **Chinese imports of refined nickel register gains of over 50% in March** The latest data by the China Non-ferrous Metals Industry Association (CNI-A) suggests that Chinese imports of refined nickel increased by 44% to 44,544 tonnes over the first three months of the year. In March, imports were also up by over 50% month-on-month and year-on-year, at 19,193 tonnes. ###### **Tightness on the supply-side may be coming to an end…** Alongside demand, the supply-side of the nickel market has also been picking up. According to the WBMS, global mine production registered positive growth of 0.7% over the first two months, which took total output to 230,700 tonnes. Every region quoted by the organisation, with the exception of the Americas on the back of labour problems, noted positive growth. H Notably, the Americas recorded a substantial fall of 31% year-on-year. The region continued to be beleaguered by industrial action at Vale’s Canadian operations. However, the company has called in “outside” workers to increase its output, and it has recently been reported that Vale is holding talks with the union to resolve the almost one year long strike. Meanwhile, the WBMS paints a different pictu

Although this estimate may seem somewhat conservative, our forecast on the reemergence of Chinese nickel pig iron production will partially offset the increase to demand. In terms of prices, since the start of May we have seen these correct from inflated levels. Although, the reversal can, in part, be attributed to the metals inherent volatility, it has also been driven by funds, which have pulled out of the base metals complex in fear that markets will drop further as problems in various European economies get worse. In the short-term, this trend may continue until economic problems get resolved. GFMS believe that there is even the possibility that prices may slip to $20,000/tonne. However, for the year as a whole, we are forecasting nickel to average $22,395/tonne. Scenario B, which would see prices average just over $25,000/tonne in 2010, would be conditional on a sharp rebound in nickel demand continuing.
